newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Credit Lyonnais faces tough EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais faces tough EU talks.

text.p: The European Commission, which will shortly receive a French request for permission to rescue Credit Lyonnais for the third time in four years, said on Thursday it would put tough conditions, including further asset disposals, onany new state subsidies.

"Assets will have to be sold, there is not a shadow of a doubt about that. There will be conditions and they will be tougher; nothing could be more logical," the spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said.
He was responding to a flood of questions from reporters eager to hear about the new plan expected to reach the Commission this week.
The spokesman said he did not know how much more money the French state was proposing to inject into the state-owned bank to ready it for privatisation.

But taking into account some nine billion francs in losses from the selling of assets, imposed by the Commission in 1995, and a 3.9-billion-franc emergency aid agreed last year, the bank would need no less than 19 to 20 billion francs, he said. He declined to elaborate.
French newspapers have reported that Lyonnais will need a total of 30 billion francs.
The French government announced it would file the new Lyonnais plan with the Commission this week but the spokesman said it had not arrived on Thursday morning.
The Commission will need three to four months to assess the new measures, he said.
It will be the third time since 1994 that the French government has bailed out the Lyonnais, which was once Europe's largest bank.

In 1995, the Commission approved a three-year restructuring programme involving a total of 45 billion francs in state subsidies. The plan consisted mainly of ridding the bank of some 130 billion francs in loss-making assets.

In return, the Commission insisted that the bank sell off at least 35 percent of its foreign assets by 1998 including a substantial part of its European banking network. It is unclear how much of this has been achieved.
Van Miert warned in October, when the Commission agreed to the emergency aid, that he would be looking for further divestments which should be "real and substantial".
